The net revisions of the previous two months to the nonfarm payroll report are a popular metric in gauging the labor market's trend.
-
*US OCT. TWO-MONTH PAYROLL NET REVISION ADDS 84,000

The top panel (blue) shows cumulative two-month payroll revisions.

The bottom panel shows the two-month net revisions.

For years, net cumulative revisions (top panel) declined, potentially signaling that the underlying labor market trend was weaker than initially reported.

But consider these cumulative net revisions
* 2025 (Jan to Sept) = -998K
* 2026 (Jan to Sept) = -28K

If negative revisions are slowing, maybe the underlying trend of the labor market is improving?

note_tweet.text:
I’ve just finished reading William Hogeland’s book on Hamilton.

As a hard-core admirer of Hamilton since the early 1990s, and someone who has long regarded him as the greatest of the Founding Fathers, I think it is a brilliant book, even though Hogeland sets out quite deliberately to demolish Hamilton’s highly romanticized current reputation. He  shows that Hamilton’s ambitions were not particularly democratic, although I suspect many of us already knew that, and had long thought that, for all his genius, or perhaps precisely because of it, he would have made a dangerous president who would have undermined democratic institutions. Nonetheless, the book confirms, even more than many of the more favorable accounts, just how brilliant, far-seeing, and hard-working a figure he was.

In a way, it is also a very good explanation of why democracy is simultaneously so grubby and yet the best of all political systems. It is built around institutional adjustment, a system that may seem messy but that. effectively prevents any one individual or group from taking the country too far in any direction.

Democracy may not be especially efficient in the short term, but it is incredibly efficient in the long term. Even a genius like Hamilton, with his extraordinary gifts, ferocious energy, powerful allies, and formidable reputation, could not take the country too far down a dangerous road. Other countries could learn from that.

The book has also greatly increased my interest in Albert Gallatin, the great opponent of Hamilton, whose statue in front of the US Treasury I have always resented. In Hogeland’s telling, he turns out to have been a great builder and rather like Hamilton himself.

P.S. Interesting trivia. It seems that the body of Charles Atlas was the model for both Hamilton's statue and Gallatin's statue.

Altman, Hassabis, and Amodei are the ones doing massive corporate lobbying at the moment.
They are the ones who are attempting to perform a regulatory capture of the AI industry.
You, Geoff, and Yoshua are giving ammunition to those who are lobbying for a ban on open AI R&D.

If your fear-mongering campaigns succeed, they will *inevitably* result in what you and I would identify as a catastrophe: a small number of companies will control AI.

The vast majority of our academic colleagues are massively in favor of open AI R&D. Very few believe in the doomsday scenarios you have promoted.
You, Yoshua, Geoff, and Stuart are the singular-but-vocal exceptions.

like many, I very much support open AI platforms because I believe in a combination of forces: people's creativity, democracy, market forces, and product regulations.
I also know that producing AI systems that are safe and under our control is possible. I've made concrete proposals to that effect.
This will all drive people to do the Right Thing.

You write as if AI is just happening, as if it were some natural phenomenon beyond our control.
But it's not. It's making progress because of individual people that you and I know. We, and they, have agency in building the Right Things.
Asking for regulation of R&D (as opposed to product deployment) implicitly assumes that these people and the organization they work for are incompetent, reckless, self-destructive, or evil. They are not.

I have made lots of arguments that the doomsday scenarios you are so afraid of are preposterous. I'm not going to repeat them here. But the main point is that if powerful AI systems are driven by objectives (which include guardrails) they will be safe and controllable because *e* set those guardrails and objectives.
(Current Auto-Regressive LLMs are not driven by objectives, so let's not extrapolate from their current weaknesses).

Now about open source: your campaign is going to have the exact opposite effect of what you seek.
In a future where AI systems are poised to constitute the repository of all human knowledge and culture, we *need* the platforms to be open source and freely available so that everyone can contribute to them.
Openness is the only way to make AI platforms reflect the entirety of human knowledge and culture.
This requires that contributions to those platforms be crowd-sourced, a bit like Wikipedia.
That won't work unless the platforms are open.

The alternative, which will *inevitably* happen if open source AI is regulated out of existence, is that a small number of companies from the West Coast of the US and China will control AI platform and hence control people's entire digital diet.
What does that mean for democracy?
What does that mean for cultural diversity?

*THIS* is what keeps me up at night.

note_tweet.text:
Weekend hack: HackerTube. I was annoyed with YouTube's recommendations so I had Claude filter down 43M comments over 20 years of HN to 6,454 videos that keep being recommended. *Significantly* better viewing experience, ~2 hours with Opus 5.5:
https://t.co/JIhXN7OSh1

- Excellent recs without any logins (state is kept in local browser session)
- Thumbnail is a representative frame from middle of the video instead of the super duper A/B test hyper-optimized user uploads
- Underlying data from the comment analysis as one zip file, point your Claude at it and ask for your own version
- HackerTube Longs ✊

A bit more on the process:
I use Claude Code (desktop app for Mac), Opus 5.5 on Medium effort as my default. I only talk to Claude and have it do everything, the only "manual work" I helped with in tandem was in the browser (reminiscent of MenuGen): 1) I had to create some kind of API key from Google Cloud UI to query YouTube for video metadata, 2) I booted up a VPS box for serving and 3) I bought the domain name. Once the box was up I gave Claude the IP and told it update, secure, harden, deploy and optimize the code, and it did the whole thing.

Many awesome projects that would have normally taken weeks/months even can now be few-shotted for breakfast. What else are we not thinking of.

note_tweet.text:
Democrats' Senate win may deliver the strongest check yet on Trump's push to reshape the Fed. Until now, checks on the longstanding institutional relationship ("Fed independence") have been piecemeal: Tillis's blockade, Powell staying on as a governor, and court rulings that kept Lisa Cook in her seat for now.

Trump got his new chairman, Kevin Warsh, this spring, but a majority of the Fed board was appointed by other presidents. There are no vacancies and should there be any, a future nominee would need to win confirmation by a Democratic Senate.

That raises a question: Does the Venn diagram of "Fed pick who can satisfy Democrats' independence concerns" and "nominee acceptable to Trump" have any overlap? No Democrat voted in favor of Stephen Miran's confirmation or for Miki Bowman's promotion to vice chair for bank supervision last year. Warsh won just one Democratic vote, from Fetterman.

Unfortunately, it wasn’t a serious proposal and it would have been bad for the state. There is definitely a version of it that would pass. I voted against this proposal, but I would vote for a different version with some of the following: 

1. Recurring tax. Why is it one time? If we’re going to tax billionaires, I want it to be a regular and predictable tax. 

2. Much smaller. 5% of assets is huge since it counts illiquid stocks and shares of private companies. Less than 1%. Has to be big enough to matter but small enough that the billionaires stay. 

3. The earmarks for healthcare pissed me off. Healthcare is such a scam industry. I don’t trust them. 

4. The state has poor governance and there is little doubt that the money would be wasted. 

5. I don’t like the retroactive aspect of it. Maybe for the first year it would make sense but only should measure liquid assets available at that time. 

6. The tax should only be paid when wealth is liquidated or realized. That test should include using the shares for loan collateral, transfers to trusts, and a strong enforcement mechanism to ensure the tax actually works. Robust anti-loophole language. 

I personally think investment income should be taxed at the same or higher rates than labor income. It is absurd how low tax rates are for the richest and how high they are for the poorest. That is not something that a state tax measure can really fix. It’s a national problem and it needs a national solution.
